newsitem.title: INDIA: India abolishes state control on coffee growers.
newsitem.headline: India abolishes state control on coffee growers.

text.p: India said on Saturday it was abolishing with immediate effect a quota control on coffee growers under which they were obliged to sell 30 percent of their output to a state-run pool.
The quota had covered 98 percent of growers, with only some small growers being granted exemption from the rule.

Coffee growers would no longer be required to pool their output for auction by the state-run Coffee Board in the domestic and export markets, junior Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah told a news conference.

"After going into all aspects of the pooling policy and noting the enhanced capability of the Indian growers to market their own coffee without government intervention, the government has decided to abolish the pooling mechanism altogether," the Commerce Ministry said in a statement.
"In other words, the free sale quota will be 100 percent for all growers from now on," the statement said.
"This has been done to with a view to further encourage growers to increase production of this commodity and exploit the vibrant international market." Ramaiah said.
But the government said it would continue to maintain a close watch over coffee prices and take appropriate steps to stabilise the market whenever necessary.
"The government also intends to enhance suitably the ceiling for duty of customs, for coffee, being exported out of India," the statement said.
It said money raised from the duty would be used for research and development by the Coffee Board to boost output to 300,000 tonnes by 2000.
In 1995/96 (October-September) India is expected to produce 223,000 tonnes of coffee against a target of 200,000 tonnes.
Coffee growers had urged the government to change a 50-year-old law authorising the Coffee Board to handle most coffee marketing activity.

"Now that the marketing function (of the board) has been removed, we will be re-focussing much more on research and development as well as helping Indian exporters to develop the international market for Indian coffee," said Phillipose Matthai, chairman of the Coffee Board.

Ramaiah said the total area under coffee production had increased to 292,500 hectares in 1995/96 from 92,500 hectates in 1950/51. Productivity had increased to 860 kg per hectare from 204 kg per hectare over the same period.
In fiscal 1995/96 (April-March), India exported 168,000 tonnes of coffee worth $430 million compared to 137,395 tonnes worth $350 million 1994/95, Ramaiah said.
